name: Vod
catalog_quote: All the Balto-Finnic languages appear to have fixed initial primary accent. ... The (nearly) extinct language Votic (Ariste 1968) appears to have secondary accents on odd-numbered syllables. Also, final syllables can take secondary accent irrespective of whether they are heavy or light, except for case suffixes, which are never accented.

new_statements.quote: 2.4. Ударение. Ударение динамическое, несмыслоразличительное, падает на первый слог, единственное исключение paráika ‘сейчас’, где вычленяется aika ‘время’ и, видимо, в прошлом проклитика.
new_statements.translation: 2.4. Stress. Stress is dynamic, non-distinctive, and falls on the first syllable; the only exception is paráika 'now', in which aika 'time' can be segmented out and which apparently was a proclitic [construction] in the past.
new_statements.citation: Agranat, Tatiana B. 2007. Zapadnyj dialekt vodskogo jazyka (Unificirovannoe opisanie dialektov ural'skix jazykov). Moscow-Groningen. [NOT in the works list; found already held by the project in our check folder from an earlier reading]

Identity: title page 'Татьяна Б. Агранат, Западный диалект водского языка, Москва-Гронинген', the Western dialect (J = Jõgõperä, L = Luuditsa subdialects), i.e. Votic. Two further passages in the same work support the reading: §4.1 p. 50 'Ударение в paraika.. падает на второй слог, притом что обычно оно бывает только на первом слоге' (stress in paraika falls on the secon…
new_statements.relation_note: Describes the Western dialect of Votic (Jõgõperä and Luuditsa subdialects, J and L). Same placement as the catalog's StressTyp2 alternating stress from the left (initial stress); adds that stress is dynamic and non-contrastive and names the single exception paráika.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is always on the first syllable (dynamic, non-contrastive); one lexical exception, paráika 'now', where the stress sits on the aika 'time' element.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated in §2.4; p. 37 adds that vowels in post-tonic (non-initial) syllables reduce, the more so the farther from the stressed syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: paráika 'now' (stress on the second syllable, from a former proclitic + aika 'time'); §2.4 calls it the only exception.
new_statements.identity_note: Agranat 2007 describes the Western (Jõgõperä/Luuditsa) dialect of Votic; Markus & Rozhanskiy 2019 (the wrong-item article actually behind the listed open link) describes Liivtšülä-Luuditsa Votic. Both are the last-speaker varieties of Western Votic; the catalog record is for Votic as a whole.

audit.deciding_source_year: 1999 (resting on Ariste 1968; primary statement held in Ariste 1948)
audit.reasoning: Quote check: both deciding sentences (vdH, Hendriks & van de Weijer 1999:449, 450) found verbatim in the chapter text we hold (filed under arch1244/src). More importantly, the held primary Ariste 1948 Vadja keele grammatika §16 (pp. 19-20), the Estonian original of the Ariste 1968 grammar that StressTyp2 and vdH cite, states first-hand: primary stress normally on the first syllable (exceptions: a few opaque compounds like para-ika and the newest Russian loans), strong secondary stress on the 3rd (and 5th) syllable with examples carrying it on word-final odd syllables, and no evident secondary stress on case endings. That is exactly the catalog alternating stress from the left plus the case-suffix fence the record already carries, and it independently refutes StressTyp2's primary-only decode (the 'contra' note stands). downloaded now: Agranat 2007 (192-pp. grammar, ILING RAN open PDF) p. 33 confirms
